video_title: Nobody Agrees What a 'World Model' Is — Justin Johnson (World Labs) Explains Why
gist: World Labs co-founder Justin Johnson argues the AI field has no agreed definition of 'world model' — at least four distinct research threads (implicit world knowledge, the reinforcement-learning POMDP formalism, generative world creation, and theory-building) are being called by one name — and proposes a POMDP-grounded taxonomy of renderer / planner / simulator to sort them. He details World Labs' two shipped bets, Marble (explicit Gaussian-splat worlds from a single image) and RTFM (implicit real-time pixel generation with no 3D representation), and argues explicit 3D wins on low compute budgets while implicit pixel-only models are what scale to infinity. He sees no need for a transformer replacement, locating the open problems instead in loss functions and very long context (millions to tens of millions of tokens).

insights.claim: Justin Johnson, co-founder of World Labs, says the AI field has no shared definition of 'world model' — there is no property or input/output signature that makes a model definitionally a world model — and this ambiguity is itself the source of confusion in the space.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Treat 'world model' claims in company pitches and research announcements as unfalsifiable marketing until the specific input/output signature is disclosed — competing products under that label may not be substitutes at all.
insights.quote: There isn't a clear definition of world models that everyone in the field agrees on. And I think that's causing part of the confusion

insights.claim: Johnson separates at least three live meanings of 'world model': implicit world knowledge inferred from a model's outputs, the reinforcement-learning POMDP state-transition predictor, and a generative model that produces navigable worlds — and says all three are legitimate systems worth building, but need different names.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: A three-way taxonomy is a due-diligence checklist: ask which of the three a startup is actually building, since capital requirements and end markets (robotics vs. content generation) diverge sharply between them.
insights.quote: we should probably build all of them as a community. Um but we should probably come up with better terms so that we don't confuse each other by calling different systems by the same term.

insights.claim: In the academic literature over roughly the past year, 'world model' has narrowed to mean a real-time interactive video model specifically, even though the broader meanings remain in use commercially and colloquially.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Papers benchmarked as 'world models' are increasingly measuring real-time interactive video quality — a narrower yardstick than robotics or 3D-reconstruction buyers actually need, so paper SOTA may not transfer to those markets.
insights.quote: the academic literature in the last year like the world model has more coalesed into a particular flavor of a of a of a like real-time interactive video model

insights.claim: Johnson identifies a fourth and far harder notion — 'world model as theory builder,' a system that produces compact explanatory theories of the world rather than just observations — and states that nobody has a credible angle on how to build it.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Discount any 'AI scientist' or automated-discovery pitch that assumes theory formation falls out of scaling generative models — a leading practitioner says the research path does not exist yet.
insights.quote: a world model should not just be directly thinking about observations but should be building deep explanatory theories about the world

insights.claim: Johnson argues that a perfect generative video model would still not deliver what scientists actually want, because the value sought is new understanding of the world rather than the pixels themselves — a capability gap that scaling video generation does not close.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Sets a ceiling on the addressable market for video-generation scaling: the enterprise/scientific value pool requires a different capability than the one being scaled.

insights.claim: The host proposes that a language model capable of building theories would not hallucinate, because theory-level reasoning would let it self-correct inconsistencies between what it generates and what it knows.
insights.speaker: Sam Charrington (host)
insights.so_what: Frames hallucination as a missing-capability problem rather than a data-quality problem — relevant to whether hallucination-mitigation tooling is a durable category or a stopgap.

themes.theme: POMDP Formalism and the Ambiguity of 'State'

insights.claim: The original technical definition of a world model comes from the POMDP literature in reinforcement learning: a model that takes the current world state plus the agent's action and predicts the next world state.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: This is the only definition with a precise, testable specification — use it as the baseline when evaluating technical claims, since anything looser is a different product category.
insights.quote: if we're in this POMDP setting then a world model is something that inputs the world state inputs the action the the agent takes and then predicts what the what's the next world state

insights.claim: Johnson argues the POMDP abstraction of agent, action, state and observation is useful well outside reinforcement learning — behavior cloning in robotics trains via supervised gradient descent with no reward signal yet still deploys into the same agent-world loop.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Robotics companies can reach POMDP-style deployment without RL infrastructure — meaning demonstration-data collection, not reward engineering, is the binding cost constraint for many robot-policy players.

insights.claim: Johnson rejects the idea that world state means every atom in the world: even in physics the right state representation is chosen relative to the abstraction needed for the problem — wave function, Newtonian particles, ion concentrations, or an idealized gas.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Fidelity is a product decision, not a physics requirement — companies claiming they must reach atom-level simulation to be useful are likely mis-scoping their compute budget.
insights.quote: even if we're talking about like ground truth state, it's always like relative to the abstraction like the abstraction that's necessary for solving the problems you care about

insights.claim: A second, distinct notion of state is now in play — a learned neural vector that behaves as if it were ground-truth state (supporting observation prediction and action-conditioned transitions) without corresponding to any physical quantity.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Learned latent state removes the need for ground-truth 3D or physics data, which is the scarce input — a key reason the implicit camp can scale on abundant video data.

insights.claim: Johnson maps the explicit-vs-learned state distinction onto model-based versus model-free RL, and says the field does not yet know which approach will win — which is precisely why he considers world modeling a more attractive research area than language modeling right now.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Open technical questions mean talent and research attention will keep flowing toward world models — but also that no incumbent has a defensible recipe advantage yet, unlike in LLMs.
insights.quote: language modeling feels like we kind of have a set of best practices that work pretty well

themes.theme: Explicit 3D vs Implicit Pixels: The Top-Level Fork

insights.claim: Johnson frames the central architectural decision in world generation as explicit 3D (build a 3D representation, then render it to pixels) versus implicit (a model generates pixels directly with no intermediate 3D bottleneck) — a fork that precedes any discussion of specific techniques like Gaussian splats.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: The cleanest way to segment world-model startups and to predict their cost structures: explicit-3D players carry rendering/asset pipelines, implicit players carry inference-time GPU costs.

insights.claim: Johnson predicts the implicit pixels-only route is the approach that scales to infinity given enough data and compute, while explicit Gaussian splats are the right choice under low compute budgets or embedded deployment because they are consistent by construction.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Implies long-run compute demand skews toward the implicit camp (large training runs plus heavy inference-time cost), while explicit-3D approaches occupy the edge/embedded and cost-sensitive tier.
insights.quote: But if you can scale up and use a lot of data and use a lot of compute, then I actually think that the the implicit 3D route is going to is going to be the thing that scales up to infinity.

insights.claim: Johnson explicitly reframes the explicit-vs-implicit debate as an engineering trade-off rather than a philosophical divide — the choice depends on the design constraints of the problem at hand, which is why World Labs has shipped both approaches.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: A vendor betting exclusively on one branch carries technology risk that a dual-track player does not; World Labs' hedge is a deliberate competitive posture, not indecision.
insights.quote: If you want cheap and consistent by construction, gausian splats are very appealing. If you want, you know, something that scales to infinity and has, you know, can rely on infinite data, infinite compute

insights.claim: Consistency in generated worlds — the property that a scene looks the same when you look away and look back — ultimately comes from training data showing consistent views of the world, not from architecture or from the choice of representation.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Data acquisition of multi-view consistent footage is the real moat in world generation, ahead of model architecture — watch who is buying or capturing 3D-consistent video corpora.
insights.quote: I mean, I think it basically comes from your data ultimately, right?

insights.claim: Implicit models have no mathematical guarantee of consistency — they achieve it only through sufficient scale, data and architectural expressiveness — whereas explicit 3D representations guarantee it structurally.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Explains why implicit world models fail unpredictably at small scale: buyers needing reliability today should prefer explicit 3D, while implicit approaches remain a scale bet.

themes.theme: Gaussian Splat Mechanics and Emerging Ecosystem

insights.claim: Gaussian splats beat triangle meshes for neural pipelines specifically because of differentiability: moving a triangle causes discontinuous jumps in the rendered image, while splats are smooth and partially transparent so gradients pass cleanly into a neural network's parameters.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: This is the technical reason decades of triangle-mesh graphics tooling does not transfer to generative 3D — an opening for new tooling vendors built around splat pipelines.
insights.quote: it's a it's a graphics representation that integrates with neural networks really cleanly

insights.claim: A Gaussian splat is a point with XYZ position, an opacity between 0 and 1, an RGB color, spherical harmonics encoding view-dependent color for reflections and gloss, plus a size and covariance matrix that determine how stretched or squashed the ellipsoid is.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Concrete per-point payload size drives storage and bandwidth economics for any product shipping splat worlds to consumers or devices.

insights.claim: A splat file-format ecosystem has emerged, with PLY as the popular but inefficient uncompressed format and SPZ as the lossy compressed alternative — Johnson analogizes the pair to PNG versus JPEG.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Format standardization is an early sign of a maturing 3D content stack — watch which format wins as a proxy for who controls the splat distribution layer.
insights.quote: ply is a pretty popular file format for gausian splats which is u you know relatively easy to read and write but pretty inefficient

insights.claim: The original pitch that Gaussian splats could be sparse — large splats covering big surfaces — has not held up: in practice sparse splats produce low quality, so splats must be fairly dense over the covered geometry.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Density requirements raise the real memory and compute cost of splat worlds above early projections, weakening the 'cheap representation' argument at high quality tiers.
insights.quote: in practice that's usually ends up in pretty low quality. So usually you want the the splat to be fairly dense over the geometry that you want to cover

insights.claim: Johnson draws a sharp line between optimization-based Gaussian-splat reconstruction — fitting a point cloud to a thousand captured images with no generalizable knowledge — and a trained world model that outputs splats from arbitrary inputs; only the latter contains a model.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: A crisp test that separates 3D-capture tooling from actual world-model companies: does it work from a single image it has never seen, or does it need hundreds of views of that exact scene?
insights.quote: There's no generalizable knowledge here and that's actually very different from what we're doing in Marble.

themes.theme: World Labs' Product Stack: Marble and RTFM

insights.claim: World Labs ships two contrasting systems: Marble, a live product at marble.worldlabs.ai that generates explicit Gaussian-splat worlds from text, images or video, and RTFM (real-time frame model), published as a research blog post in late 2025, which generates pixels in real time with no explicit 3D representation.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: World Labs is hedged across both branches of the technology fork — one commercialized, one at research stage — which is a different risk profile from single-approach competitors.
insights.quote: you can definitely try out Marvel. Um that's our our product at marble.worldlabs.ai. You can sign up and and play around with that today.

insights.claim: Marble's pipeline generates a 360-degree panorama image as an intermediate step from the user's input, then lifts that panorama into a full 3D Gaussian-splat world.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: The panorama intermediate is a disclosed architectural detail competitors can replicate, and it explains Marble's single-viewpoint-centric output characteristics.
insights.quote: one intermediate step in that is generating a 360 panorama image

insights.claim: Marble's marquee and best-performing use case today is single-image input: the model matches the visible content and generates a plausible completion for everything outside the frame, then lifts the whole scene into navigable 3D.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Single-image-to-world drops the content-creation cost floor dramatically versus multi-view capture rigs — the key unlock for consumer and indie-game adoption.
insights.quote: the kind of marquee use case is almost single image and that's probably what works best in marble today

insights.claim: The same Marble backend model produces both photorealistic real-world rooms and fantastical video-game-style environments from a single image or prompt, because it was trained on real-world, fantastical, photorealistic and non-photorealistic data together.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: One general model spanning realistic and stylized output means World Labs addresses both enterprise digital-twin and games/entertainment demand without separate model lines.

insights.claim: Splats are World Labs' lowest-common-denominator output format: the raw model output is splats, from which the team renders images and video or fits a triangle mesh, because game engines and VFX engines still do not work well with splats today.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Mesh export is currently mandatory for professional pipeline integration — engine-side splat support is a gating dependency for adoption in games and VFX.
insights.quote: in in some contexts like you want to import this into into a game engine or or VFX engine, sometimes those those don't work so well with splats today

insights.claim: Explicit 3D data is a rare and scarce data type, so World Labs trains heavily on abundant 2D images and video — which are projections of a 3D world — rather than being bottlenecked on native 3D corpora, even though the target output is 3D.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Removes 3D-data scarcity as a barrier to entry, which weakens the moat of anyone whose advantage rests on a proprietary 3D scan library.
insights.quote: even if you want a model that at the end of the day is going to produce 3D, it's still very powerful for it to learn on large quantities of image and video data

insights.claim: World Labs' published taxonomy sorts world models by which element of the POMDP loop they output: observations (renderer), actions (planner), or states (simulator) — reframing apparently unrelated research programs as different views of one system.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: A one-question classifier for any world-model company — what does it output? — that maps directly to end market: content, robotics, or simulation.
insights.quote: pretty much everything that people is are training today that are called world models are usually outputting one of three things in that in that loop

insights.claim: Renderers like Genie and RTFM and robot policy planners are near-perfect duals of one another: the renderer takes actions from a human and outputs observations, while the planner takes real-world observations and outputs actions.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Duality implies capability transfer between generative-video and robotics labs — advances in one camp are more portable to the other than the current market segmentation assumes.
insights.quote: So the renderer and the planner are kind of like almost perfect duels to each other.

insights.claim: Johnson says nobody has yet nailed the simulator category — a model that maintains and evolves an explicit or semi-explicit world state in response to actions — making it the most open of the three buckets.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: The clearest white space in world models today; a working action-conditioned state evolver would be a genuine step change rather than an incremental result.
insights.quote: I actually don't think anyone's nailed that one right now.

insights.claim: Marble already straddles the renderer/simulator boundary because users see pixels but the model actually outputs Gaussian splats — an explicit state you can measure distances in and insert object assets into, capabilities a pure pixel renderer cannot offer.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Explicit state unlocks editability and measurement — the features enterprise and production workflows actually pay for, and a concrete differentiator versus pixel-only competitors.
insights.quote: Because it's an explicit 3D representation, you can measure the distance between two points or I can insert or I can manipulate the state explicitly by pulling in another object asset and putting it into that world.

insights.claim: Johnson predicts that within a couple of years single unified world models will combine renderer, planner and simulator capabilities in one shared trunk of parameters, with different input and output heads selecting the mode per application.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: If capabilities converge into one trunk, specialized single-mode vendors face substitution risk from a general world model in the same way task-specific NLP models were absorbed by LLMs.
insights.quote: but I think over the next couple years, we'll start to see models that combine more and more of these capabilities into one powerful unified uh model

insights.claim: Johnson warns his own taxonomy is deliberately non-rigid — real-world systems blend the categories, and adhering to the framework too strictly would be a disservice.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Useful caution against over-indexing on category labels when comparing products; the boundaries are already leaking in shipping systems like Marble.

themes.theme: Architecture Bets: Transformers, Loss Functions, Long Context

insights.claim: Johnson says no architectural step function is required for world models — transformers are powerful, scale well and work across data types — pushing back on the recurring claim that world models demand a post-transformer architecture.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Supports continuity in the existing transformer-optimized hardware and software stack; bearish for narratives that a new architecture will reset the compute-vendor landscape.
insights.quote: no transformers are great. Transformers are super powerful. They scale up really well.

insights.claim: Johnson locates the genuinely open question in the loss function rather than the architecture — diffusion versus rectified flow versus discrete autoregression — noting that the GAN-to-diffusion shift was a change in loss function, not in architecture.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Reframes where research surprise is likely to come from; a loss-function shift can invalidate a competitor's training recipe without invalidating its hardware or serving stack.
insights.quote: we used to do GANs now it's diffusion like that's a kind of a change in loss function more than it is a change in architecture

insights.claim: Johnson argues long context is the one area needing real architectural evolution: world models routinely require hundreds of thousands to tens of millions of tokens of context, turning what was a nice-to-have in LLMs into the everyday problem for any scaled world model.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Points demand at long-context attention research, memory bandwidth and KV-cache-heavy inference hardware — a distinct infrastructure profile from today's LLM serving.
insights.quote: it's very quick very easy to get situations where you want hundreds of thousands or millions or tens of millions of tokens of context for different world modeling problems

insights.claim: There is no settled definition of a token in world models: depending on the architecture it may be a 16x16-pixel patch across four video frames, a bundle of Gaussian splats, a voxel chunk of 3D space, or an opaque learned latent — an area Johnson expects continued divergence.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Token-count and context-length comparisons across world-model vendors are not apples-to-apples, so headline context numbers should not be used to rank systems.
insights.quote: So some architectures a token is literally like a little patch of a video.

insights.claim: Johnson is skeptical of geometric deep learning and baked-in symmetry priors for spatial models, arguing hard symmetry assumptions get you 80% or 90% of the way but break down, and that the repeated deep-learning lesson is simple representations with scaled-up models behind them.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: Bearish for research programs and startups whose differentiation rests on inductive biases and structured priors rather than scale and data.
insights.quote: those like hard assumptions of symmetry maybe get you maybe 80% or 90% of the way there, but they're going to break down eventually

insights.claim: Johnson advises against bottlenecking through an explicit 3D representation when the desired output is images or video — choose the representation adapted to the actual task, since complex intermediate representations are harder to optimize and less likely to work at scale.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: A design rule that predicts consolidation toward end-to-end pixel models for entertainment and video use cases, with explicit 3D reserved for cases needing editability or measurement.

insights.claim: Johnson says no good canonical learning resource on world models exists yet — no lecture series or book he can recommend — which is part of what World Labs' taxonomy blog post was written to address.
insights.speaker: Justin Johnson
insights.so_what: A sign of how early the field is: no canonical curriculum means talent pipelines are thin and hiring for world-model expertise stays expensive.
insights.quote: I wish I could recommend a better lecture series or or or book or something on world models, but I I just I don't think anyone's written down anything super awesome yet
